## Emerging Directions and Architecture Synthesis: Looped Depth, `#linebreak()`{=typst}Design Tradeoffs, and How to Read What Comes Next {#sec-ch8}

*One More Tradeoff, Then a Framework for Every Tradeoff After It*

### Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- Distinguish distinct block parameters from effective block
  applications ($L_{\text{distinct}}$, $T_{\text{passes}}$,
  $L_{\text{effective}}$), and explain why depth-wise weight sharing
  does not reduce compute or automatically reduce/share KV-cache
  state.
- Distinguish depth recurrence (looped transformers) from sequence
  recurrence (ch. 6's Mamba/SSM state) and from fixed-vs-adaptive
  computation, and distinguish a paper's described behavior from a
  released implementation's actual behavior.
- Apply a 10-question synthesis framework to a new, unseen model,
  citing chapters 1-7 by name instead of re-deriving their mechanisms.
- Propose a defensible mechanism combination for a stated design
  constraint, stating which effects follow from architecture alone and
  which still require benchmarking.

### Why architecture keeps evolving

Chapters 2 through 7 each taught one tradeoff: a resource traded for a
complication. New mechanisms keep appearing faster than any workbook
can catalog, so this closing chapter teaches one more tradeoff family
(looped depth) at full depth, then gives a compact, reusable framework
for reading whatever comes next, rather than a wider catalog.

### Recurrent depth / looped transformers

A looped transformer applies **depth recurrence**: the same block
weights run repeatedly over an *evolving hidden state*. This is not
**sequence recurrence** (ch. 6's Mamba/SSM state, carried across token
*positions*, [@src-37]) -- the two are called "recurrent" casually but
are different mechanisms.

$$
L_{\text{effective}} = L_{\text{distinct}} \times T_{\text{passes}}
$$

$L_{\text{distinct}}$ (distinct block sets stored) and
$L_{\text{effective}}$ (block applications executed) answer different
questions: reusing weights across $T_{\text{passes}}$ lowers
$L_{\text{distinct}}$ relative to $L_{\text{effective}}$, but compute
still happens for every application, and shared weights imply neither
shared intermediate activations nor one shared KV-cache across passes
-- each pass may need its own cache entries unless an architecture
adds cache reuse deliberately.

![Looped vs. unrolled depth. Panels 1-2 use the same 22 distinct
blocks; panel 2 just runs them twice. Panel 3's unrolled view shows 44
block applications, but applications sharing a color share the same
underlying weights -- distinct parameters (22) and block applications
(44) are different counts. Per-application cache icons are schematic,
not a claim that caches are
shared.](figures/rendered/fig-looped-vs-unrolled-depth.svg){#fig-looped-vs-unrolled-depth}

**Two verified examples, different loop policies.** Mixture-of-Recursions
([@src-40], Bae et al., 2025) is a *research proposal*: a router
assigns adaptive, per-token recursion depth, and the paper itself poses
a caching choice ("recursion-wise caching" vs. "recursive sharing")
with different memory consequences -- weight sharing alone does not
resolve which one a real deployment uses. Nanbeige4.2-3B ([@src-42],
2026-07-27) is a *released, open-weight model*: a fixed two-pass loop
over a 22-layer stack (44 total block applications), chosen to raise
effective depth under a fixed parameter budget, not per-token adaptive.
These are not the same design -- do not treat "looped" as one policy.

::: {.callout-note}
Public reporting has associated recurrent depth with "GPT-6 Astra,"
but no official technical source confirms this architecture -- this
workbook does not treat that proprietary architecture as verified.
:::

### Fixed versus adaptive computation

| Design | Idea | Benefit | Complication |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fixed loop count | every token gets the same passes | simple, predictable batching | no conditional savings |
| Adaptive halting | model estimates whether another pass helps | conditional compute | training stability, variable execution paths |
| Token-level recursion routing | different positions get different depths | fine-grained conditional compute | routing decisions, batching inefficiency, cache management |

: Adaptive methods do not always save compute -- a released implementation may compute all passes before selecting an exit even when a paper describes early exit {#tbl-fixed-vs-adaptive}

### Worked example: looped vs. conventional depth

$L_{\text{distinct}}=22$, $T_{\text{passes}}=2$ (matching Nanbeige4.2-3B's
own reported loop policy), so $L_{\text{effective}}=44$, compared
against a conventional 44-distinct-block stack. Illustrative equal-
per-block-size assumption (verified programmatically, not Nanbeige's
own exact per-block parameter split):

| Quantity | Looped | Conventional | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Distinct blocks | 22 | 44 | -- |
| Block applications/token | 44 | 44 | 1.0 (equal) |
| Block-parameter storage | 1.1B | 2.2B | 0.5 |
| Complete-model parameters | 1.6B | 2.7B | 0.59 |

: Block-parameter ratio is exactly $1/T_{\text{passes}}$; the complete-model ratio is NOT exactly 0.5 -- embeddings/output heads/routers add the same mass to both totals {#tbl-looped-worked-example}

Cache caveat: separate pass-specific cache entries may make cache
requirements comparable to 44 block applications, not 22, unless an
additional cache-reuse mechanism is used (ch. 7's cache/state
category).

### MTP: a bridge, not a destination

::: {.callout-note}
Standard training predicts token $t{+}1$; multi-token prediction adds
objectives/modules for further offsets ([@src-43]). These auxiliary
components may be removed at inference, or -- a separate design
choice -- repurposed to propose draft tokens. Proposing tokens does
not by itself define the complete speculative-decoding algorithm
(acceptance/rejection, lossless-distribution guarantees, draft-model
scheduling): that belongs to a future inference workbook. MTP's
*training* treatment belongs to a future pretraining workbook. Neither
is taught here.
:::

### Architecture synthesis framework

For any new model, ask:

1. What is reused?
2. What is activated conditionally?
3. What state grows with context?
4. What state is compressed or bounded?
5. How many distinct parameters are stored?
6. How many block/module applications run per token?
7. What communication is introduced?
8. Which behavior is architecture-defined?
9. Which behavior depends on training?
10. Which claimed benefit still needs benchmarking?

![Every mechanism from ch. 1-7, plus looped depth, sits under the one
resource/behavior it primarily changes. MTP bridges off the map to two
future workbooks instead of sitting under a resource-axis header --
it is a training-time choice, not itself the speculative-decoding
algorithm.](figures/rendered/fig-architecture-decision-map.svg){#fig-architecture-decision-map}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"Reusing the same layers gives the depth of a larger model at the
compute and cache cost of the smaller model."** False in three parts:
distinct parameter storage may be smaller, block applications still
execute (compute is not reduced), and pass-specific K/V or state may
still be required (cache is not automatically shared).
:::

### Applied exercise

A team wants a long-context model under a weight-memory constraint,
but can afford additional computation for difficult tokens; serving
must support moderate concurrency on multiple GPUs. Candidate
mechanisms: GQA, MLA, sliding/local attention, MoE, hybrid recurrent
layers, looped depth, adaptive recursion. Propose one combination and
state: its weight-memory, cache/state, compute, and communication
effects; one training complication; one thing that must be
benchmarked; and one tradeoff that cannot be inferred from the
architecture alone. There is no single correct combination.

### Interview lens

*"Compare scaling a transformer by adding distinct layers, looping a
shared stack, and using adaptive recursion. Discuss parameters,
computation, KV state, batching, and implementation complexity."* A
strong answer keeps distinct parameters, block applications, and
cache/state as three separate quantities across all three scaling
choices, and names batching/implementation complexity as separate,
non-architectural costs.

### Chapter recap

@fig-architecture-decision-map is this workbook's visual recap: every
mechanism from chapters 2-7, plus looped depth, in one place.

- $L_{\text{effective}} = L_{\text{distinct}} \times T_{\text{passes}}$
  -- distinct parameters and effective compute are different
  quantities; weight sharing lowers the first, not the second.
- Shared weights across passes do not imply a shared KV-cache; cache
  reuse across passes is an additional, separate design decision.
- Fixed loop counts, adaptive halting, and token-level recursion
  routing are three different policies with different training and
  serving complications -- a paper's described behavior and a released
  implementation's actual behavior are not guaranteed to match.
- MTP is a training-time bridge to two future workbooks, not itself
  the speculative-decoding algorithm.
- The 10-question framework reads any new model without re-deriving
  chapters 1-7's mechanisms.
- Architecture constrains but does not determine benchmark quality or
  latency alone -- this has been every chapter's closing caution, and
  it is this workbook's last one too.
